name: Post-fascism
scope: Post-fascism, as the defining sources use it, names a movement or party that comes out of fascism and now works within electoral democracy while keeping a core of ultranationalist, exclusionary politics. Two strands are named. (1) The Italian strand (Fini's 1993 self-description 'not neo-fascist, but post-fascist', the MSI's turn into Alleanza Nazionale at Fiuggi in 1995, read by Griffin as a modernised national-rebirth project, and its heir Brothers of Italy), taken from Brown and Newth, Puleo and Piccolino, Ortiz Cabrero and Sierp, Pileggi and Chielli. (2) Tamás's wider concept (Boston Review 2000; Autonomies 2018): post-fascism fits global capitalism and electoral democracy, drops the Führer, one-party rule and paramilitaries, and keeps fascism's central move of removing citizenship from groups of people. Brown and Newth treat it as a discursive logic rather than a full ideology; it is not a party platform in general. Pre-war and neo-fascist movements, and populist radical right parties that no source ties to the term, are out of scope.

summary: Post-fascism is the term for movements and parties that descend from or echo fascism but work within electoral democracy, chiefly Italy's Alleanza Nazionale after the 1995 Fiuggi turn, and in Tamás's wider sense an anti-immigration, ethnicist politics without one-party rule. Its defining sources describe a discursive logic and a political break rather than a programme, so few statements are settled.
notes: Themes searched in the defining sources: party rule and democracy, antifascism and totalitarianism (Fiuggi theses), immigration, nation and rebirth, economy, family and morality, institutions (presidentialism). Only four statements are stated directly. Presidentialism at Fiuggi is reported but does not settle direct election of the head of state. Griffin (1996) and Newth and Maccaferri (2022) could not be opened and are cited only second-hand. Old answers drawn from the 2022 Brothers of Italy programme were nulled: it is not a key work.
